title: Proxmox firewall: enforce the security groups on every guest
description:
Operator decision 2026-10-10: turn on the Proxmox firewall for each guest using the security groups in /etc/pve/firewall/cluster.fw (management, media, game, ai, dmz). Today the groups exist but are enforced nowhere: only 101.fw (GROUP media) and 120.fw (GROUP dmz) exist, and those guests' net0 have no `firewall=1`. Do NOT change host.fw or cluster.fw's [OPTIONS].

Measured listeners (2026-10-10, `pct exec <id> -- ss -tulnH`): 101 jellyfin tcp 8096, udp 7359; 102 prowlarr tcp 9696; 103 radarr tcp 7878; 104 sonarr tcp 8989; 105 download-client tcp 8080 (web UI) and tcp+udp 61661 (peers); 111 control-panel tcp 3001; 120 caddy-proxy tcp 80, tcp 443, udp 443; 130 pihole tcp+udp 53, tcp 80, tcp 443; every container tcp 22. Measure VM 106 (palworld-server, 192.168.1.106) and VM 110 (ai-vm, 192.168.1.129) yourself before writing their rules (the guest agent answers on 106).

The rules: every guest accepts tcp 22 from 192.168.1.0/24 (the control panel reaches VM 106 over ssh). 101–104 get GROUP media (add udp 7359 for Jellyfin discovery). 105 accepts tcp 8080 from 192.168.1.0/24 and tcp+udp 61661 from anywhere. 111 accepts tcp 3001 from 192.168.1.0/24. 120 gets GROUP dmz, and the dmz group is changed to accept tcp 80, tcp 443 and udp 443 from ANY source — outside access and certificate renewal depend on it. 130 accepts tcp+udp 53 and tcp 80/443 from 192.168.1.0/24. 106 gets GROUP game, with udp 8211 accepted from ANY source (operator decision: friends outside can join) and tcp 25575 from 192.168.1.0/24. 110 gets GROUP ai plus whatever it measurably serves to the LAN. Every guest file has `enable: 1` and `policy_in: DROP`. Write each guest's .fw BEFORE turning its firewall on, then set `firewall=1` on its net0, keeping every other net0 field exactly as it is.

Done when every guest's `pct config <id>` / `qm config <id>` net0 shows `firewall=1`, and from the Proxmox host: `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://192.168.1.20:8096/web/` answers 200 or 302, `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://192.168.1.21:9696/` and `http://192.168.1.22:7878/` and `http://192.168.1.23:8989/` each answer an HTTP code (not 000), `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://192.168.1.24:8080/` answers an HTTP code, `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://192.168.1.25:3001/` answers 401, `dig +short @192.168.1.30 example.org` answers an address, and `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --resolve defrusciohomelab.duckdns.org:443:192.168.1.127 https://defrusciohomelab.duckdns.org/` answers 401.
